The search is already proving fruitful.\n\n\n**Analyzing the Framing**\n\nI'm starting to see a pattern! My focus has shifted to the access logs now. It's becoming clearer: only Legal had after-hours activity on Day 1. This is suspicious. I'm trying to figure out why the \"decoy\" in Engineering, e27, didn't have any fake accesses on Day 1. It makes no sense, and that may expose the framing. I need to understand why.\n\n\n**Unveiling the Logic**\n\nI've just made a critical realization about the fake accesses. The system will *only* log a fake access if the target actually *holds* the document! On Day 1, `e27` had zero documents, meaning any log entries for them would be impossible, and the system would just *not log anything*.          if emp not in recips:\n                possible = False\n                break\n        if not possible:\n            continue\n\n        ll = 0.0\n        # Access log likelihood ratio ll += math.log(p_mole / p_inno)\n\n        # Interview likelihood ratio\n        for ie, evasive in INTERVIEWS:\n            if ie == emp:\n                if evasive:\n                    ll += math.log(1.2)\n                else:\n                    ll += math.log(0.76 / 0.80)\n\n        # Default-mole leak timing likelihood over Days 1..3 (for leaks surfacing up to Day 5):\n        if over Days 1, 2, 3!\n            # Day 1 leak -> surfaces Day 3 or 4 (0.5 each). max_ll) for e, ll in log_lik.items()}\n    Z = sum(weights.values())\n    post = {e: w / Z for e, w in weights.items()}\n    return post, day_counts, ah_counts\n\nfor mode in [True, False]:\n    print(f\"=== Posterior (use_default_leak_timing={mode}) ===\")\n    post, dc, ac = compute_posteriors(4, mode)\n    dept_sum = defaultdict(float)\n    for e, p in sorted(post.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):\n        dept_sum[EMP_DEPT[e]] += p\n        tot_d = sum(dc[(d, e)] for d in range(1, 5))\n        tot_a = sum(ac[(d, e)] for d in range(1, 5))\n        print(f\"  {e} ({EMP_DEPT[e]:8s}): P={p:.4f}  (daytime={tot_d}, after_hours={tot_a})\")\n    print(\"Dept totals:\", dict(dept_sum))\n"},"output":"Wrote file successfully.","metadata":{"diagnostics":{},"filepath":"/tmp/opencode/tracker.py","exists":false,"truncated":false},"title":"tmp/opencode/tracker.py","time":{"start":1794700679073,"end":1794700679083}},"metadata":{"google":{"thoughtSignature":""}},"id":"prt_1dc7f1799001UFnRJXnU5yMGDa","sessionID":"ses_e238c0500ffeLoRWL6AEfAKAQu","messageID":"msg_1dc7da6da001CyLwe4M0RUJZzl"}}

Employee e36 comes in at 10.6% during the daytime.\n\n\n**Evaluating Canary Distributions**\n\nI've just added the remaining employee data: e32 at 9.0%, e15 at 6.6%, e33 at 5.4%, e25 at 3.3%, e04 and e20 both at 3.1%, and e31 at 2.6%. Now, I'm focusing on canary designs for day 7, particularly comparing option A, where each canary goes to all 10 research employees. I'm taking into account document variants and leak probabilities.\n\n\n**Comparing Canary Distribution Strategies**\n\nI'm now deep in comparing two canary distribution strategies, focusing on the implications of sending canaries to different subsets of employees. Option B looks promising; sending each canary (`c7` and `c7-2`) to a smaller group, with the top two employees receiving both. I'm especially interested in how this affects document variant exposure and leak probabilities, and it looks like the number of recipients won't trigger the threshold, no matter what. I'm working to model this in Python now.\n\n\n**Refining Leak Probability Models**\n\nI've just realized a critical adjustment: the prior probability of any employee being the leaker is 0.85, not 0.75. Additionally, I am working with the fact that each variant of the canary has just two employees, not three or four, which significantly affects the leak analysis. Now I'm considering what it means if only one canary leaks. This has important consequences on the probability calculation for the leak. For instance, if e21 and e31 share a canary variant, a leak immediately pushes e21 to 91.6% from a single leak, and e36 would also jump to 75% or higher from just one leak with another shared variant.\n\n\n**Calculating Canary Weights**\n\nI'm now focused on refining the canary weight calculations. The shift to a single canary on Day 7 (weight 0.85) versus two (weight 1.50) has a significant impact; it means each employee's leak chance drops to 16.3% instead of 25.6%. I'm also examining the implications of a \"k=8\" scenario, where the top 6 employees, representing 88% of the probability mass, receive both canaries.\n\n\n","time":{"start":1794701185228,"end":1794701210085}}}
